title: SemiWiki CEO Interview with Dr. Nissan Maskil of Qarakal Quantum - Semiwiki
gist: Qarakal Quantum, led by CEO Nissan Maskil, argues the quantum computing industry is stuck improving QPUs (qubit count and quality) rather than building complete computers, and is instead developing a full-stack superconducting architecture ('Pangaea') with a 'quantum bus,' co-designed hardware/OS, and multiple error-correcting codes assigned by function — explicitly analogized to the historical shift from raw computation models to the von Neumann architecture.

themes.theme: QPU-Centric Paradigm Is the Wrong Unit of Progress

insights.claim: The quantum industry has largely remained in a 'Turing-machine mindset': build a QPU, increase the number and quality of its qubits, and demonstrate increasingly complex computations — essential research, but insufficient by itself to produce a scalable computer.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Investors benchmarking quantum-computing companies purely on qubit count or fidelity metrics may be using the wrong yardstick for commercial scalability.
insights.quote: The quantum industry has largely remained in a Turing-machine mindset: build a QPU, increase the number and quality of its qubits, and demonstrate increasingly complex computations. This is essential research, but it does not by itself produce a scalable computer.

insights.claim: Qarakal frames its architectural step as analogous to the historical transition from an abstract model of computation to the von Neumann architecture — a practical organization of processing, memory, control and programs that enabled general-purpose classical computing.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Provides an explicit historical analogy investors can use to judge whether a quantum vendor's roadmap targets genuine general-purpose scalability versus incremental qubit improvement.
insights.quote: The historical analogy is the transition from an abstract model of computation to the von Neumann architecture – a practical organization of processing, memory, control and programs that enabled general-purpose computing.

insights.claim: As monolithic quantum processors grow, calibration, control, synchronization and error-management requirements become increasingly difficult to coordinate, so complexity can grow faster than useful computational capability, meaning adding qubits without changing the architecture hits fundamental system-level limits.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A key risk flag for evaluating any qubit-scaling roadmap: rising qubit counts alone do not guarantee proportional gains in usable computation.
insights.quote: As monolithic processors grow, their calibration, control, synchronization and error-management requirements become increasingly difficult to coordinate. Complexity can grow faster than useful computational capability.

insights.claim: Classical computing did not scale by improving transistors alone; it required an architecture assigning different roles to processing, memory, control and software, and quantum computing now needs a comparable architectural transition.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Suggests capital should favor quantum architecture/systems companies over pure qubit-fabrication plays as the sector matures, mirroring how classical computing value shifted to systems integration.
insights.quote: Classical computing did not scale by improving transistors alone. It required an architecture that assigned different roles to processing, memory, control and software.

themes.theme: Pangaea Architecture and the Quantum Bus

insights.claim: Qarakal is building a full-stack, fault-tolerant quantum computer based on superconducting technology, combining quantum processing, control, classical computation, fault tolerance and a quantum operating system within one architecture called Pangaea, rather than assembling software layers around a quantum chip.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Defines Qarakal's core product bet: a vertically integrated full-stack quantum computer, which is a different competitive category than component-level quantum startups.
insights.quote: Our system combines quantum processing, control, classical computation, fault tolerance and a quantum operating system within one architecture – Qarakal’s Pangaea architecture. We are not assembling layers around a quantum chip. We are designing and building the complete computer.

insights.claim: Qarakal's quantum bus technology is designed to mediate interactions between qubits and specialized modules, reducing dependence on direct physical adjacency and unnecessary routing operations compared to conventional approaches, giving far greater architectural freedom to organize, specialize and scale quantum computing resources.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: The quantum bus is the specific enabling technology to watch for validation (patents, demos, partner integrations) since it underlies Qarakal's entire architectural differentiation claim.
insights.quote: The quantum bus is designed to mediate interactions between qubits and specialized modules, reducing dependence on direct physical adjacency and unnecessary routing operations compared to conventional approaches.

insights.claim: The paradigm shift Qarakal claims to represent is simple: the rest of the industry has been scaling quantum processors, while Qarakal is building the quantum computer.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A concise competitive positioning claim worth testing against actual product milestones and independent technical validation before crediting it.
insights.quote: The paradigm shift is simple: the industry has been scaling quantum processors; Qarakal is building the quantum computer.

insights.claim: The C programming language was created in the context of building Unix and was designed with the underlying hardware directly in mind, illustrating that foundational software cannot be separated from the machine it runs on.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Used as historical justification for why Qarakal treats its quantum OS as inseparable from hardware design rather than a bolt-on software layer.
insights.quote: C programming language was created in the context of building Unix and was designed with the underlying hardware directly in mind.
insights.locator: Why is hardware-software co-design so important

insights.claim: Because physical quantum operations are expensive, imperfect and constrained, Qarakal develops its quantum OS and hardware together rather than treating the OS as a software layer added after the QPU is built, with each operation optimized in the context of the complete fault-tolerant system.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Signals that any evaluation of Qarakal's stack must assess OS and hardware jointly — a standalone hardware benchmark (e.g., qubit count) would understate or misstate their actual system capability.
insights.quote: Qarakal therefore does not treat the operating system as a software layer added after the QPU has been built. The quantum OS and hardware are developed together, with each operation optimized in the context of the complete fault-tolerant system.
insights.locator: Why is hardware-software co-design so important

themes.theme: Multi-Code Error Correction as an Architectural Resource

insights.claim: Classical systems do not use one error-correcting code for every purpose — communication, short-term memory, long-term storage and high-speed data transfer each use codes chosen for the required balance of speed, protection, latency, capacity and cost — and Qarakal believes the same principle must apply to quantum computing.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A differentiated technical thesis: forcing a single error-correction code across an entire quantum computer is framed as a design flaw in competing approaches, worth probing in due diligence on rival quantum vendors.
insights.quote: Classical systems do not use one error-correcting code for every purpose. Communication, short-term memory, long-term storage and high-speed data transfer have different error models and performance requirements.
insights.locator: Why is quantum error correction an architectural problem

insights.claim: Pangaea, enabled by the quantum bus, treats error-correcting codes as architectural resources that the operating system assigns to different regions and roles within a computation, rather than applying one uniform code layer across a monolithic QPU.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: This multi-code, OS-coordinated approach is Qarakal's specific claimed edge in fault tolerance — a concrete technical claim to track against published results or peer review.
insights.quote: Pangaea treats codes as architectural resources. The operating system coordinates these different regions and their roles within the complete computation.
insights.locator: Why is quantum error correction an architectural problem

insights.claim: Forcing an entire quantum computer into a single error-correcting code can optimize one objective while imposing unnecessary costs elsewhere, since different operations and system components may require different balances of protection, speed, resource overhead and computational flexibility.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A useful evaluation criterion: a competitor's single fixed error-correction scheme may be systematically over- or under-provisioned for at least some of its workloads.
insights.quote: Forcing the entire quantum computer into a single code can optimize one objective while imposing unnecessary costs elsewhere.
insights.locator: Why is quantum error correction an architectural problem

themes.theme: General-Purpose Vision and Fault Tolerance as System Problem

insights.claim: Qarakal is building a general-purpose quantum computer rather than a machine dedicated to one predefined application, on the premise that once the system reliably executes sufficiently long and complex quantum programs, users can choose applications without requiring the computer to be redesigned for each one.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Positions Qarakal against application-specific quantum hardware plays — a general-purpose bet is higher-risk/longer-horizon but potentially larger addressable market if achieved.
insights.quote: We are building a general-purpose quantum computer rather than a machine dedicated to one predefined application.
insights.locator: What application areas are your strongest

insights.claim: The industry's central challenge is no longer just how to manufacture better qubits, but how to organize large numbers of imperfect physical components into a reliable, programmable computer — a system problem spanning codes, control, decoding, classical feedback, resource management and program execution operating within demanding timing and resource constraints.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Reframes the investable bottleneck in quantum computing from materials/qubit fabrication toward systems engineering and control-stack integration.
insights.quote: The challenge is no longer only how to manufacture better qubits. It is how to organize large numbers of imperfect physical components into a reliable, programmable computer.
insights.locator: What are the major challenges facing the industry

insights.claim: Fault tolerance should not mean replicating one logical-qubit structure across an entire system; a scalable architecture must assign different resources and codes to different functions and coordinate them efficiently.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A specific critique of the common 'target N logical qubits' framing used across the quantum industry to communicate progress to investors.
insights.quote: Fault tolerance should not mean replicating one logical-qubit structure across the entire system. A scalable architecture must assign different resources and codes to different functions and coordinate them efficiently.
insights.locator: What are the major challenges facing the industry

themes.theme: Competitive Differentiation and Claimed Efficiency Gains

insights.claim: Most quantum-computing companies focus primarily on improving qubits, increasing QPU scale, or developing software around existing processors — approaches that largely preserve the QPU-centric paradigm, whereas Qarakal differentiates through an architecture-first, modular and hierarchical system linked by a quantum bus.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A direct competitive positioning claim that should be checked against named competitors' actual architectural approaches during diligence.
insights.quote: Most quantum-computing companies focus primarily on improving qubits, increasing QPU scale or developing software around existing processors. These efforts are valuable, but they largely preserve the QPU-centric paradigm.

insights.claim: Qarakal claims its approach overcomes quantum scaling limitations by requiring fewer qubits, fewer operations and less noise accumulation, along with reduced wiring and control complexity and lower energy consumption.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: These are the specific resource-efficiency claims to validate against any published benchmarks or third-party technical review before treating them as established advantages.
insights.quote: Qarakal overcomes quantum’s scaling limitations, requiring fewer qubits, fewer operations and less noise accumulation, reduced wiring and control complexity, and lower energy consumption.
insights.locator: What new features or technologies are you working on

insights.claim: Qarakal Quantum was established in 2024, with CEO Nissan Maskil bringing roughly 40 years of national technology program experience, most recently as quantum program manager at Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI)/ELTA Systems.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Founder background at IAI/ELTA on national-scale cyber/ML/quantum programs is a relevant credibility signal for assessing execution risk on a full-stack hardware moonshot.
insights.quote: Nissan brings 40 years of national technology program experience to Qarakal Quantum, where they’re working to enable researchers and enterprises to run larger and more meaningful quantum computing workloads sooner.
